analysis.one_liner: Raises required overtime pay from time-and-a-half to double time.
analysis.headline: The bill to double overtime pay was introduced in the Senate in August 2026 and referred to committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 so that employers must pay hourly and other covered workers two times their regular rate — instead of the current one and one-half times — for hours worked beyond 40 a week. It would take effect 180 days after being signed into law. It would raise pay directly for millions of workers who put in overtime, at a cost of higher labor bills for their employers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who regularly put in overtime hours — hourly employees and lower-paid salaried workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act — would see overtime pay jump from 1.5 to 2 times their regular rate. Workers at businesses that rely on long overtime shifts (manufacturing, logistics, health care, construction) would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: Changes the required overtime rate in the Fair Labor Standards Act from 'one and one-half' to 'two' times the regular rate, including for the specific overtime exceptions listed in section 13.
Sets the effective date 180 days after enactment, giving employers roughly six months to adjust before the higher rate applies.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who rely on overtime — manufacturers, logistics and shipping companies, hospitals and health systems, restaurants, construction firms — would face higher labor costs for every overtime hour. Some would respond by hiring more staff, restricting overtime, or raising prices. Workers whose hours get cut in response could lose income even as the rate rises.

drawbacks.text: The 50-cent premium on every overtime hour is a direct cost increase for employers, which could respond by cutting overtime hours, hiring more part-timers to avoid overtime, automating, or raising prices — so some workers might see fewer overtime hours even at a higher rate.

The bill makes no transition adjustments or phase-ins beyond the 180-day delay, and does not change who is exempt from overtime, so workers who are currently exempt from the FLSA's overtime rules would see no benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who keep their overtime hours, this is a straightforward pay raise on every overtime hour — an extra 50% of regular pay above what they currently get. The cost falls on the businesses employing them, and the main honest objection is that businesses may restructure hours so some workers end up with fewer overtime hours. For workers whose overtime is steady, the gains clearly outweigh those risks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on August 5, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has not taken further action.

narrative.text: Senator Ruben Gallego introduced the Double the Wage for Overtime Act of 2026 on August 5, 2026, joined by four Democratic cosponsors — Senators Blumenthal, Markey, Merkley, and Van Hollen.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action is recorded.
The bill text amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to replace 'one and one-half' with 'two' as the required overtime rate, effective 180 days after enactment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers relying on heavy overtime keep paying time-and-a-half instead of double, saving them the difference; overtime workers keep the lower rate.

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to double the FLSA overtime rate and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Edward Markey, Jeff Merkley, and Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters are Democrats and the bill has no Republican cosponsors; no opposition action is recorded, so the split has not yet been tested.

industries.industry: Employers that rely on heavy overtime (manufacturing, logistics, hospitals, construction)
industries.note: The bill would raise the cost of every overtime hour from 1.5x to 2x regular pay. Businesses could absorb that by cutting overtime hours or raising prices, which is why the industry's interest in keeping the current rate runs against workers' interest in higher pay.
Workers with steady overtime would get double pay on every overtime hour, a direct raise in take-home pay, unless employers cut hours in response.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with no committee action recorded and no Republican cosponsors. Most labor bills at this stage in a closely divided chamber do not advance to a floor vote; unless the HELP Committee schedules a markup or it is attached to a larger bill, it is likely to expire at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
